pages.name: The Veska Reveal — Reading the Chops

text.content:
Veska's notary office. The chops do not match — and they were never supposed to.

The set-piece scene where Veska Maelan reads the recovered evidence and names the people behind it. The single most important investigative beat in Phase 3 — everything afterward unfolds from what Veska tells the party here.

Setup

The party brings their evidence to Veska's notary office on Whalemarket Quay. Depending on travel approach, the meeting happens differently:

  • Quiet Pursuit: An evening session, hours of careful work. Veska closes the office, brings up the back-room lamp, makes tea twice. The reading takes most of a night.
  • Commercial Cover: Two daytime sessions, second and third visits. Veska works in business hours only; the readings are interrupted by walk-in clients she cannot turn away without arousing suspicion. Two to three hours per session.
  • Official Delegation: Veska is gone. Her former apprentice Hella Voren (after the agreed phrase is spoken) hands the party a sealed packet of Veska's notes and chop-rubbings. The notes are read in the party's lodging, by lamplight — not the reading below, which she gives in person to documents she has in front of her, but the version under On the Official Delegation road, which the party lays their own documents against. Her notes give the three details of the letter E in words, so nothing the Hand-off needs is lost; only her sketch and her certainty are.

Read aloud (Quiet Pursuit and Commercial Cover; the delegation's notes are below)

"Set them on the table for me. The escrow first. Then the coin. Then the lacquered tube and the seed pouch. The ledger fragment goes here, between the lamp and my elbow. Yes. That is how I will read them."

(She works in silence for some time. Lenses on, lenses off, lenses on. Tracing chops with one careful finger, holding rubbings to lamplight, comparing hands. When she is ready she does not announce it; she simply begins.)

"The escrow's house seal is the firm's, the public one. That tells you nothing. Anyone with the firm's wax could press it.

The Hardby clearing-chop in the lower-left margin was applied by Solen Mereth. He runs the bond-loading office at the Hardby branch. I know his hand the way you know the shape of your own kitchen at night. He will not have signed it elsewhere — he is too careful — but I have three other documents in my files where his chop sits next to his hand on the same page, and I will give you those for comparison.

(If Gilst's bank instrument from Loftwick is on the table, she lays it beside the escrow.) "And this is his too — the same chop, the same hand, a season earlier. One reading covers both."

The marginal endorsement — Hold for V., or his agent of record, against presentation — is in a different hand. Smaller. Older. I have seen it three times in the last four years and I have never been able to put a name to it from a single document. But."

(She lifts the escrow into the lamplight. Holds it there for a long moment.)

"If you ask me whose hand this is, and you give me until the end of this week to lay it next to the only three other examples I have, I will tell you it is Tarlith Vhal Sereth's. And if I am wrong, I am wrong by one office. He is the senior partner at Cindren and Vhal Rel Astra who has not signed a letter at his own desk in eleven years. The firm pretends he is unwell. He is not unwell. He is hiding what he writes."

(She sets the escrow down. Picks up the coin.)

"Now look at the countermark. Tower above three waves. The firm has struck seven of these over its history, one live in each office of record and the rest retired. They are supposed to be unique to their offices and identical within the firm. This one — see the chip on the lower-right wave — is the Hardby stamp. I know it because I notarized its replacement in 579 CY. Solen brought me a new stamp for the firm's records and asked me to certify the old one as destroyed. I notarized the certification. I assumed the old one was destroyed. I assumed wrong. The old stamp, the chipped one, the one this coin was weighed in on — that stamp is in the upstairs strongroom of the Hardby branch tonight, and it has been there for five years.

The vellum strip with the four words. Harbor before throne. That is older language. It is from the Aerdi Concordat of the Bay, the imperial settlement that established the harbor commissions. It says, in plainer Common: when there is no king sitting and confirmed, the harbor councils run themselves and run their cities. It is a clause about timing. Whoever wrote those four words on that vellum is telling someone — telling Solen, I think — that the seating of a harbor council before a throne is settled is the lever that will work."

(She lifts the seed pouch, holds it to the lamp, sets it down.)

"The seeds are display, not stock. The treatment to make them look fresh is alchemical. Whoever bought this pouch did not need to grow grain — they needed grain to look grown. The dry barony Vandrell was carrying these for is in South Province, but the receipts the conspiracy has written on grain it never grew clear through Hardby's weighbridge. Tamsin Moraven was within a month of being able to prove it."

(She closes her ledgers. Folds her hands on the desk.)

"You came here for names. I will give you four.

One. Solen Mereth, head of bond-loading at the Hardby branch. He chopped the escrow. He kept the defect-stamp. He runs the second set of books at the branch level. He is the operational lever.

Two. Tarlith Vhal Sereth, senior partner at Rel Astra. He wrote the marginal endorsement. He is the one whose name a court must hear if any of this is to mean anything outside this room.

Three. Anver Resh, freelance broker, formerly Solen's clerk. You will find him at the Coopered Wreck most evenings. He hires people for things the firm cannot put in writing. He is the man Sarth was given by.

Four. There is a fourth. I do not have the name. I have a hand — the hand that wrote one further annotation in the last set of records I saw, two months before they stopped letting documents I could see cross my desk. That hand is not Sereth's. It is not Solen's. It is not Resh's. It is not anyone in Hardby. It is the hand that the firm answers to. (If the Loftwick instrument is on the table:) The three small initials countersigning that instrument are the same hand — the same letter, three more times. I do not know whose it is. I will tell you, before you leave for Rel Astra, the things I do know about how that hand writes the letter ‘E.' That is all I have. Make of it what you can."

On the Official Delegation road — what the notes say

Veska fled before the party arrived and never saw their escrow, their coin or their tube. Hella Voren's packet is what Veska knew, written for a reader she expected never to meet. Do not read the reading above on this road; read this, silently or aloud, in the party's lodging by lamplight.

Six sheets in a notary's small upright hand, numbered, and a fold of chop-rubbings pinned to the last.

The first sheet is Solen Mereth: the Hardby clearing-chop as he applies it, rubbed from three documents in her own files where his chop sits beside his hand on the same page, with the dates. "Lay any paper he has chopped beside these. The lower-left corner is his habit. He will not have changed it."

The second is the stamp: a certificate she notarized in 579 CY, copied out entire, by which Solen Mereth certified the old Hardby countermark stamp destroyed and a new one struck — and her note in the margin that the old stamp's lower-right wave carried a chip, and that she has since seen that chip on coin weighed in after 579. "If you hold a coin with the chip on it, you hold a thing that officially does not exist, and it was weighed in by his office."

The third is three documents she has seen in four years, all payouts to one private clearing account, all endorsed in the same small hand that is not Solen's — described letter by letter, with the account's number. "I believe the hand is Tarlith Vhal Sereth's, senior partner at Rel Astra, who has not signed a letter at his own desk in eleven years. I cannot prove it from three. A fourth would do it."

The fourth is a name: Anver Resh, formerly Solen's clerk, "who hires for the firm what the firm will not write down. Hardby knows him as Tarsh." No haunt and no address; she writes that he will have been moved before anyone reads this.

The fifth is the Concordat clause, harbor before throne, in the words she would have used across the table: when there is no king seated and confirmed, the harbor councils run their cities, and whoever seats a harbor council before a throne is settled has found the lever that works.

The sixth is the shortest. A hand she saw once, on one further annotation, two months before the firm stopped letting documents cross her desk; not Sereth's, not Solen's, not anyone's in Hardby. She writes out three things about how it makes the letter E — the loop, the serif, the angle of the descender — and nothing else, because she has nothing else.

Then the party does what she would have done. The escrow's clearing-chop against Solen's three rubbings: Investigation DC 12, or any notary on the Quay for a fee (Therion Halask does it again, properly, in Rel Astra). The chip on their coin's lower-right wave against her margin note: no roll. The marginal endorsement against her description of the small hand: Investigation DC 14, and it matches. What this road loses is her certainty, her opinion under seal and her sketch; what it keeps is every fact the Hand-off needs. Her sworn notes, attested as hers by the Quay clearing-house, stand in for the opinion on every later page — and the subpoena, not Veska, is how the party gets the blotter and the stamp's record.

What the party leaves with

  • Names: Solen Mereth, Tarlith Vhal Sereth, Anver Resh.
  • Veska's prepared notarial opinion identifying the Hardby chop, the defect-stamp, and (with comparison documents) the Sereth marginal endorsement. This is the document that turns the recovered evidence into a legally admissible package in Aerdi or Yeomanry court.
  • The fourth-hand "E." observation. Veska does not name Eclavdra. She cannot. She knows only that there is a fourth hand the firm answers to, that this fourth hand signs what it annotates with a single capital initial, and that the letter is "E." She will give the party her observations on how the letter is formed — three small details about the loop and the serif and the angle of the descender — that may, much later, let the party recognize the hand again. On the Official Delegation road they are written out in her notes instead; that road loses only the sketch. Phase 3 does not name Eclavdra. Veska does not know to name her. Hold this thread.
  • The harbor-before-throne reading. Veska gives the party the operational frame for the phrase. They will need additional Hardby investigation (Zoria Weis, the Gynarchy's harbor commission registry) to confirm what the conspiracy is positioning toward, but the frame is set: seat the harbor before the throne.

If they bring the circular (First Travel Intermission)

A party that came by sea may put the Grey Fee's circular on her table with everything else. She reads it last, and briefly.

If the circular is on the table. Read after her four names, before the party goes.

"This is a fair copy." She has it under the lamp for less than a minute. "A Quay copying-house hand, round and quick. There are forty clerks on Whalemarket who write like this for a copper a sheet, and not one of them reads what they copy."

She looks at the initial at the foot of it for a long moment and does not touch it. "Your clerk copied that too. Keep it. It will be useful to you once I have told you how the real one is made."

Once she has given them her three details, the party can lay the circular beside them and find that the copied E. matches none of them. That is the finding the intermission promised: somebody in Hardby sat down and copied out orders from a hand nobody in Hardby admits to having seen. Veska will not name a copying-house or a clerk, and if pressed she says there are forty; the copyist is a dead end on purpose. The crossed stroke in the seal she ignores. To a notary it is a sorting mark, and that is all anyone in Hardby can tell them.

What Veska does next

Quiet Pursuit: Veska continues to work in Hardby. She sends the party off with everything she has and tells them she will be here when they next need her. She is here when they next need her — through Phase 4 and beyond.

Commercial Cover: Veska finishes her opinion by the end of the week she asked for, hands it to the party on the third visit in business hours, and warns them she will close the office for "a quiet week" once they leave Hardby. She does. She survives.

Official Delegation: Veska, who fled before the party arrived, is in a coastal village two weeks east. Hella Voren passes the party one final letter from her: "If you find Tarlith Vhal Sereth, ask him about the autumn of 571. He will know what you mean. I will know also, when you write to me about it."

Tamsin Moraven, recovered. Alive, depending on the path. The picture is the artist's: in play she is on a straw mattress behind a locked door, not roped to a chair.

Outcome by travel approach

What the party finds when they pursue the Tamsin Moraven thread depends on which travel approach they chose at the end of Phase 2. None of the three is a failure state; all three carry weight.

Quiet Pursuit — Live Recovery in Hardby

Where she is

A warehouse on Black Cog Lane in the harbor district. Owned through the shell company "Greenwall & Mast" (which Zoria Weis or Veska can confirm as a Cindren & Vhal cutout). Two-story stone-and-timber warehouse, an attached caretaker's residence, an old loading dock onto the canal at the rear.

The setup

Tamsin is held in a small first-floor room that was once a clerk's office — single window (barred), wooden door (locked from outside), straw mattress, water jug, chamber pot, no light after sunset. She has been in this room since before the party left Loftwick — five weeks, near enough. (GM: how she got from Loftwick to Hardby in the eleven days before the party rode out is not a thing she can tell them. She was hooded; it was dark; there was a rope; she will not speak of it, any more than Hesren Vesh will, and no DC opens it. Let the table notice that two people made the same impossible journey. It is a Phase 7–8 payoff.) She is alive, thin, and very tired, and she has stopped expecting the door to open for any good reason. She has not been physically harmed; her captors have been told to keep her until further instruction. She has spent her time memorizing the daily schedule of the warehouse.

Captors

  • Three hired guards (use SRD Thug) on rotating shifts, two on at any time. They are paid by the week and not personally invested. They do not know who Tamsin is or why she is held; they were told "a difficult client." They will fight if attacked but will surrender if outnumbered or cornered.
  • One Cindren-aligned overseer, Reyna Worth (her sheet is a Warrior Veteran), who is the only one who knows what Tamsin is. She arrives daily at the third bell after dawn for a brief check, leaves by the fourth. She is loyal to the firm, will not surrender, and will try to kill Tamsin if she suspects rescue is imminent. Resolving Worth before she can give the order is the rescue's central tactical problem.

How the party learns where she is

Three ways on this road, so that no single NPC carries the rescue.

  • Anver Resh, cornered with leverage (@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgTarshC1]{Tarsh — The Coopered Wreck Confrontation}). The quickest, and the only one that also names Solen and Sereth.
  • Zoria Weis, asked about Greenwall & Mast: the register shows a warehouse on Black Cog Lane held under a name nobody uses. Veska can say the same of the shell, but not of the building.
  • The warehouse girl. Lerra Voss carries the prisoner's food in from the lane twice a day. A day's watch on Black Cog Lane (Perception DC 13) finds a girl going into a warehouse that ships nothing with a covered dish, and coming out without it. She is frightened, and will talk to a woman before a man: Persuasion DC 12. (On this road she is alive and in the city; the delegation's Lerra, who smuggled the letter, is the same girl a season later.)

The rescue

Best approach: enter at night when only the two thug-guards are on watch and Worth is at home. Stealth approach to the back loading-dock (DC 14), pick the rear lock (DC 15), neutralize the two guards (combat or stealth), open Tamsin's room (DC 12 lock).

Worth-mitigation: the party needs Worth's morning check not to happen. On this road there are three doors — let them pick, and let the choice cost something different each time.

  • Ailen Moraven. The sculptor's workshop on Bell Street runs apprentices, a delivery cart, and a foundry fire that is entirely real. A cart shed across a lane at the wrong hour, or a kiln that smokes badly enough to bring the ward-watch, buys the morning. The cost is that the party has to ask Tamsin's nineteen-year-old daughter to help them get her mother back, and she will say yes before they finish the sentence. This is the strongest version of the scene and the one that hurts.
  • Doral Hurst. The retired Watch sergeant at 15 Cooper's Tale, next door to the safe house. A summons from the harbormaster's office is a form he has filled out four hundred times and can still forge from memory, and Worth will answer it because ignoring one is worse than obeying one. The cost is that Hurst is a man who sends his grandson to fetch the Watch inside five minutes when something looks wrong — asking him means telling him enough truth that he stops being a friendly neighbour and becomes a witness with an opinion. Persuasion DC 15, or DC 11 if they show him Tamsin's Sevenday note from Loftwick, if they thought to copy it at Vellin's house (Phase 2, Scene 4b) — or, failing that, the carbons of her three refused queries from Ailen's bundle, which are in her hand too. Not her last letter: on this road she is alive and that letter is still in the room with her.
  • Hesp Olfair. A halfling fence in the Salters' Quarter, sixties, keeps a pawn-and-sell shop two streets back from the docks (Hesp's Borrow-and-Sell) and a very tidy set of books he would rather nobody read. He will arrange anything on this list for coin and will not ask what it is for. The cost is money — 150 gp, non-negotiable, half in advance — and the fact that Hesp now knows the party wanted Reyna Worth out of a building on a particular morning. He does not sell that today. He files it.
Whichever door they take, if Worth does not arrive for her morning check the party has clear access for at least one full day before the firm realizes Tamsin is gone.

If the party assaults during a Worth-present hour: more dangerous. Worth will try to kill Tamsin within her first round; the party must reach Tamsin's room before Worth does. Initiative matters.

After

Tamsin needs three days of rest, food, and quiet before she is fit to travel. The Mossen Place can hold her, or Brother Holst's infirmary on Cobbler's Walk for the three days of rest, or — if the party is being chased — the Bell Street cellar can hide her for a night. She must be out of Hardby within a week or the firm will find her again; see Who takes them west on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3QRefJournal.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 4}.

Live Tamsin is the strongest possible Phase 4 witness. She has been keeping mental notes on what she heard in the warehouse — names mentioned by Worth, papers carried in and out, the rhythm of the operation. She can corroborate Veska's reading and add operational detail no one else can. She will also say, unprompted, that the man who carried her queries to the firm was Joren Krill, the weighmaster; she guessed it in her first week in the room.

Commercial Cover — Live Recovery East of Hardby

Where she is

The Whitemoor Estate, a former wine-house turned coastal residence, two days east on the coast road. Held, like the Black Cog Lane warehouse, through Greenwall & Mast and two more shell companies behind it. The estate sits on a small walled headland; the coast road approaches it through a stand of pine wood. There is one main house over a wine cellar, a stable range on the west side, a gate lodge, two gardens, and a small dock on a sheltered cove below the east wall.

The setup

Tamsin was moved out here about a month ago, when Hesren Vesh had been down from Loftwick a fortnight and the firm had decided his news was real (on Quiet Pursuit the party arrives inside that fortnight, which is why she is still on Black Cog Lane). She has had a bedchamber and proper food ever since, which is its own kind of answer about what they intend. She is held in an upstairs bedchamber. She has freedom of the upstairs corridor (door locked at night) and is fed properly. She has been told nothing about why she is held but has guessed most of it. She has been at the estate long enough to know the house and grounds.

Captors

  • Five hired guards (SRD Bandit Captain and four Thugs) (six PCs: a fifth Thug), more competent than the Hardby crew. The captain is a contractor named Olo Crask, retired Aerdi marine, professional, careful. He is paid handsomely, will fight to the last, but is not personally murderous — he will not kill Tamsin without explicit order, and the order has not been given.
  • One Cindren overseer, Reyna Worth (the same Worth as the Hardby case; she travels), present at the estate one night in five: she goes out on the courier's boat and comes back on it, and spends the rest of the cycle in Hardby coordinating the firm's response.
  • One sealed-orders courier who arrives every five days from Hardby with new instruction, by boat from the third wharf, landing at the cove. The next courier is due two days after the party can reasonably reach the estate. If the party arrives ahead of the next courier, the standing order is "hold safely." If they arrive after, the new order may be "move further east" or "dispose of asset" depending on what the firm has learned.

The rescue

This is a longer operation than the Hardby warehouse, not a bigger fight: five men and a walker's lantern, a Low encounter on paper for five PCs at 6th, written to be won by reconnaissance and infiltration. The danger is Worth's night and the courier's order, not the numbers. Castrian can arrange travel to the estate's vicinity (a former lover of his, the wine merchant Aldous Varley, owns the next headland over and will host the party for a night). Veska can identify the captain Crask by reputation and brief the party on what to expect.

Best approach: arrive ahead of the next courier, scout for a day, infiltrate by sea (the dock is the weakest point and Crask has fewer guards stationed there) on the second night.

Everything needed to run the night — four ways to learn where she is, the map keys, the guards by night, the numbers, the read-alouds and the way home — is on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgWhitem1]{Whitemoor — Running the Rescue}.

After

Tamsin is in better condition than the Hardby version (she has been fed and housed properly), but the journey back is longer and the firm is more alert. The party returns Tamsin to Hardby quietly and houses her at Castrian's for two days. Then she goes west, not east: the party is bound for Rel Astra and she is bound for Loftwick, and somebody else must take her — see Who takes them west on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3QRefJournal.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 4}.

Live Tamsin is, again, the strongest Phase 4 witness. She is also visibly grateful, which lands as a quiet beat for the party — she did not believe she would be recovered.

Official Delegation — Body Recovered, Letter Smuggled

What happened

Tamsin was murdered by Reyna Worth at the Black Cog Lane warehouse five days before the party arrived in Hardby. The order came from Solen Mereth the week the delegation's arrival date was fixed and posted at the Hall of Salt and Tide — the firm had known for a season that they were coming, and waited until it knew exactly when, so that there would be nothing to find and no time to look. Tamsin was killed quickly (a single thrust); her body was placed in a barrel and dumped in the harbor; a fisherman recovered the barrel two days after that, which is three days before the party rides through the West Gate. The Hardby city watch certified the death as "harbor incident, foul play probable, jurisdiction limited."

What the party recovers

  • The body. The party can claim it through the watch (the accredited delegation has standing for foreign-national death claims). Tamsin can be returned to Loftwick for burial; Vellin and Ailen can lay her to rest.
  • Her last letter. A warehouse worker at the Black Cog Lane facility — a young woman named Lerra Voss, who served Tamsin food in the warehouse for the eleven weeks she was held — smuggled out a single folded paper Tamsin had written. Lerra has been afraid to deliver it; when the party arrives in Hardby and a known Yeomanry delegation is in the city, Lerra approaches Hella Voren (Veska's apprentice) and asks her to pass it on. Hella does. Lerra herself disappears within a week of giving the letter; her family does not know what happened to her. The party may, in Phase 4 or beyond, choose to investigate.

The letter (read aloud or printed as a handout)

Vellin and Ailen — if you read this, I am not coming home.

I want you to know that I knew what I was doing when I asked the questions, and I would ask them again. The grain that was paid for never existed. The men who paid for it knew it never existed and bought it anyway because the paperwork is a kind of weapon, and they wanted the weapon. I followed the weapon back through three counting houses to the firm, and the firm to a name in Rel Astra I could not read — a hand, not a name, on paper I was not allowed to keep. I do not know who the man is. I know only that I was asking about him when they came for me.

Vellin — there is a small lacquered box in the bottom of my wardrobe under the spare linen. Inside it, my filings on the South Province grain. Take them to the Hardby weighmaster Joren Krill, no — to Caelith Dunivar in Loftwick. Joren is not safe. Caelith is. He will know what to do with the filings. He may already know.

Ailen — your work has been the great quiet joy of my life. I have not told you this often enough. The portrait you carved of your grandmother is on my desk. I look at it every morning. If I am gone, take it back; do not let it sit in this office.

I love you both very much. I am sorry to have left you with this.

— T.

What this means for Phase 4

Without live Tamsin, the Phase 4 indictment is built on documents alone. It is still viable — Veska's sworn notes plus the recovered branch records (via subpoena) plus Tamsin's letter (admissible as testamentary evidence in Aerdi court) plus the body itself (with coronial findings of foul play) is a substantial package. But the loss is real. Treat this beat with the gravity it deserves. Vellin and Ailen carrying Tamsin's coffin home from Hardby is a cutscene that the GM should let the table sit with for as long as the table needs.

Joren Krill — the weighmaster's trade

Any live road, and the delegation if they want him. One short scene; it pays the plant on the Forward-Planting script and gives Phase 4 a Hardby voice that can sit in a Rel Astra courtroom.

Joren Krill, the Hardby weighmaster, keeps the public weighbridge office at the landward end of Whalemarket Quay and is on the firm's payroll. He is the man who carried Tamsin Moraven's queries to Solen Mereth, one at a time, and he knows what became of her. He is not brave and he is not a fool: he has watched the firm move a witness and heard what it did to a clerk in Loftwick, and he has worked out that a weighmaster who knows that much is the next thing it tidies. He wants out, and he will sell for it.

  • Finding him. The weighbridge, mornings, second to sixth bell after dawn; the Green Magpie off the Greater Market most evenings. Tamsin's unsent letter to him (Ailen's bundle) or her last letter's crossed-out line is the way to open him: show either and he goes grey. Insight DC 13 sees that he is frightened, not guilty; both are true.
  • What he sells. The weighbridge day-book for the eighteen months on Tamsin's list — which shipments cleared the bridge on paper and never crossed it, in a Hardby civic hand, admissible in any court — and the words: "I took them to Mereth. I did not know what Mereth would do." (He knew.) On the delegation road he will also say where the barrel went into the water, which closes the watch's file.
  • What he wants. A passage out of Hardby on the party's hull, east or west, and his name on the indictment as a witness, not a defendant. Persuasion DC 14 with the letter; DC 17 without it, and he sells only the day-book then, and asks for coin. He will sign nothing in Hardby. Carried to Rel Astra, he deposes for Halask (Phase 4, Path 1); sent west, he swears before Caelith.
  • The cost. Approaching him openly at the weighbridge is seen: +1 on the Pressure Clock unless the party has already decided to leave within two days. He reports to Solen until the moment he decides to trade, and the moment is the letter.

Resh names him unasked if cornered; Tamsin names him the day she is free; the delegation's letter crosses him out. If the table never goes looking, he is a name on Phase 4's indictment list and nothing more, which is what the plant promised.

Handout — Tamsin's Last Letter

Tamsin's smuggled last letter — the Official Delegation road only, where she is dead before the party lands. Lerra Voss got it out of the warehouse and Hella Voren holds it at the Quay clearing-house. On the two roads where Tamsin lives, this handout is not used; she tells them herself. Pass to the player whose PC reads it.

Tactical Map

Black Cog Lane warehouse — tactical map. For the Quiet Pursuit recovery. Tamsin is in the old clerk's office, northwest corner; its door is not drawn — put it on the office's south wall, locked from outside, and the barred window on the north. The big doors face the lane; the "rear loading dock" is the water channel down the east side. The docks map labels the building Derelict Warehouse, which is what the lane calls it.

Tactical Map

Whitemoor Estate — tactical map. For the Commercial Cover recovery. Tamsin is held in an upstairs bedchamber at the east end of the main house; the east service stair is the shortest way up to her.

Scenes (in the Phase 4 scenes compendium, because the coast road passes the estate again): @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4S1a0abdb6ed]{Whitemoor Estate Grounds}, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4Sfbb32822f3]{Whitemoor Estate Upper Floor}, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4Swmcellar01]{Whitemoor Estate Cellar}. Walled, lit, and set at night.

Whitemoor — Running the Rescue

GM page, Commercial Cover only. Everything on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgTamsin1]{Tamsin Moraven — Three Recoveries} about who holds Tamsin and why still stands. This page is how to run the night: how the party learns where she is, how they get there, the three maps keyed, the guards, the numbers, and the way home.

How the party learns where she is

Three ways, so that no single NPC carries the rescue.

  • Anver Resh, cornered with leverage (@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgTarshC1]{Tarsh — The Coopered Wreck Confrontation}). The quickest, and the only one that also names Solen and Sereth.
  • The third wharf (First Travel Intermission). The Whitemoor boat leaves at dusk every fifth day and comes back light; see @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgWharf01]{The Third Wharf and the Drafts House}.
  • Zoria Weis confirms; she does not find. Asked about Greenwall & Mast, she can show that it holds a headland property two days east, under a name nobody uses.

Getting there

Two days east on the coast road, or most of a day by sea. Castrian writes to Aldous Varley, the wine merchant on the next headland, who was something to Castrian once and is still fond of him. Varley houses the party for a night, lends them a boat and a man who knows the cove, and asks nothing. Veska, asked, knows Olo Crask by reputation: "An Aerdi marine who retired without being asked to. He holds what he is paid to hold."

Scouting from Varley's headland takes a day. Perception DC 13 counts the guards and learns the walker's round; DC 16 also notes the day the boat last came, and so when the next courier is due.

The courier, and the clock

The courier (a Spy, 2024; he carries the orders and the key and will not fight for either) lands at the cove at dusk every fifth day with sealed orders and the key to the sea door, and sails at first light. The next is due two days after the party can reasonably arrive. What he carries depends on what the firm knew when he left Hardby, which is the Pressure Clock:

  • 0–1: "hold safely." Nothing changes.
  • 2–3: "move her east." Crask takes her off by the courier's boat the next night.
  • 4 or more: "dispose of the asset." Crask will do it — that is what an explicit order means — but not before dawn, and not before he has read it twice. A party on the grounds that night still has the dark hours.

A courier taken at the third wharf or at the cove never arrives, and the order already in force stands.

The estate by night — three maps

@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4S1a0abdb6ed]{Whitemoor Estate Grounds}, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4Sfbb32822f3]{Whitemoor Estate Upper Floor}, @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-4-scenes.Scene.BR2P4Swmcellar01]{Whitemoor Estate Cellar}. All three ship walled, lit and at night; raise the light for a daylight look. The guards' routine is the same either way.

Grounds and ground floor

  • W1 The gate and lodge. An iron double gate on the drive (locked, DC 14; you can see through it) and the lodge beside it, with its own door onto the road (DC 13). One guard is on watch here all night, by the lodge fire.
  • W2 The drive. Gravel round a planted island: Stealth checks across it are made at disadvantage.
  • W3 The house. Front door off the drive (DC 14), barred inside after dark. Study, parlour, hall, dining room and kitchen; the hall's north door opens on the back lawn.
  • W4 The kitchen. The fire is banked, not out. The service stair to the upper floor is not drawn on this map; put its foot at the kitchen's east end.
  • W5 The cellar steps. An outside stair under an iron grate, in the angle between the dining room and the kitchen, with a door into the kitchen. The grate is locked (DC 14) and loud: a failed check is heard by the walker.
  • W6 The well, east of the kitchen.
  • W7 The stable range, the old pressing barn: two horses and a tack room. Nobody sleeps here.
  • W8 The kitchen garden (south-west) and W9 the formal garden (east). Low hedges, no cover worth the name.
  • W10 The east postern. A door in the east wall (DC 14). Below it a cut stair goes down the rock to the cove, the dock, and the sea door into the cellar.
  • W11 The north postern, onto the cliff path (DC 14).
  • The wall is a stone base with an iron railing along it: Athletics DC 12 to cross, and anyone on the railing is in plain sight of the walker.

Upper floor

  • U1 The master bedroom (north-west). Crask's. He sleeps light and armed with the door ajar, and the key to Tamsin's room hangs on a nail by the bed. Its north door opens on the terrace (U10).
  • U2 The linen room, up the short passage north of the hall.
  • U3 The study (north-east). Worth's, on the nights she is here: her papers, her orders, and a hard little bed.
  • U4 The hall and the main stair. A lamp burns all night at the stairhead.
  • U5, U6 The two south-west bedrooms. The guards off watch, one in each.
  • U7 The bath, down the short passage between U6 and U8.
  • U8 Tamsin's room (south-east): a bed, a desk, a fire allowed to burn low, and a window that does not open far. Locked at night (DC 13; Crask's key).
  • U9 The service stair, beside her room, down to the kitchen. The shortest way to her.
  • U10 The terrace, over the back lawn.

Cellar

  • C1 The guard post (north-west): a table, a lamp, a chest of the guards' kit. Manned only after an alarm.
  • C2 The store: coal, tools, a barrel.
  • C3 The cell (north-east): a cot, a bucket, a barred door (DC 15). Empty until the alarm goes up.
  • C4 The wine hall: four racks still half full of the old house's wine, tall enough to hide behind.
  • C5 The east passage, from the wine hall south to the stair.
  • C6 The sea door in the passage's east wall (DC 15; the courier carries the key). Behind it, the cut stair down to the cove and the dock.
  • C7 The stair (south-east), up to the cellar steps (W5).

The guards, by night

Olo Crask and four Thugs (six PCs: a fifth), on two watches that change at midnight. On watch: one at the gate lodge (W1), and one walking the grounds every half hour with a shuttered lantern — the lodge, the stable, the front of the house, the east lawn, the postern, and back. From the postern he looks down the cove stair once an hour. Off watch: two asleep in U5 and U6. Nobody watches the dock at night, and that is the weak point the scouting finds.

  • The walker. Stealth DC 12 on the grounds, at disadvantage within 15 feet of his open lantern or on the gravel of the drive.
  • In the house the boards talk: Stealth DC 13 indoors. Each failed check wakes one sleeper, nearest first; Crask wakes on the second.
  • Worth is at the estate one night in five, out on the courier's boat and back on it, and sleeps in U3. Decide, or roll a d6 the night they go in: on a 1 she is there.

If the alarm goes up

Crask's standing order is the cellar, not a knife. He and one guard take Tamsin down the service stair, out through the kitchen to the cellar steps, and into the cell (C3), and hold its door; the rest come for the noise. He will not kill her without an explicit order, and he fights to the last at that door — he is not for buying once the shooting starts.

Worth is the danger. If she is at the estate she goes for Tamsin herself, and her orders are older than Crask's: she tries to kill her in her first round within reach. On a night Worth is there, getting to U8 first is the whole rescue.

Read aloud — the cove

When Varley's boat comes into the cove on the second night.

The oars go in without a sound because Varley's man has wrapped them, and the cove opens out of the dark like a hand: shingle, a short stone jetty with one iron ring and no boat at it, and above it the headland going up black against a sky only a little less black.

There is a stair cut into the rock. You can see the first dozen steps and then you cannot. At the top of it, a long way up, the wall of the estate runs along the edge of the cliff with iron on top of it, and behind the wall the house stands with one lamp lit in an upper window and the rest of it asleep.

Somewhere above you a lantern moves along the wall, stops, and goes back the way it came.

Read aloud — Tamsin's door

When the lock gives and they open U8, whichever way they came in.

The room is warmer than the corridor. Somebody has been allowed a fire, and it has been allowed to burn down to embers. A desk with a cold lamp on it; a jug and a cup; a book face-down to keep its place. The bed has been slept in, and it is empty.

She is standing against the wall beside the window, where the door would hide her if it swung wide, with the cup held in her hand the way you would hold a stone. A woman in her fifties in a borrowed dressing-gown, thinner than her clothes were made for, with her daughter's dark hair going grey at the temples.

She looks at your faces one at a time. She knows none of them. Then she looks at what you are carrying, and at the open door behind you, and something in her face that has been shut for weeks comes slowly open.

"You're not from the firm," she says. It is not quite a question. "Who sent you?"

She comes as soon as she understands. She will want to know about Vellin and Ailen before anything else, and she should be told the truth.

The way home

Down the cove stair to Varley's boat, back to his headland before light, and to Hardby by sea the next day; then two days quiet at Castrian's (three days' rest in all before any long road). Then she goes west: see Who takes them west on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3QRefJournal.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 4}. The raid is +2 on the clock however clean it was; a missing prisoner is a report.

What Tamsin knows

  • The grain fraud in full: which shipments, which weighbridge, which years. She corroborates Veska's reading and her own list in Ailen's bundle.
  • The estate's routine, learned by heart over a month: the watches, the walker's round, the courier's day, Worth's night in five.
  • That the man who took her queries to the firm was Joren Krill. She guessed it in her first week as a prisoner, and says it now.
  • She has never heard the name Sereth. She has heard Worth say "Rel Astra wants" twice, and that is all.

She is the strongest Phase 4 witness the party can have, and she wants to go home. Both are true, and the Hand-off asks which wins.

The Coopered Wreck. Tarsh at his usual table, watching the door he sat to watch.

The set-piece scene where the party confronts Anver "Tarsh" Resh in person. Available on Quiet Pursuit (best case) or Commercial Cover (more guarded). Not directly available on Official Delegation; on that path, see the GM note at the end.

The Coopered Wreck

A long, low, coal-smoke-dark sailors' tavern on the harbor district edge — three blocks from the wharves, two from the harbor wall, one from the rope-walks. The proprietor is Olfard Trent, a one-eyed retired bosun in his sixties. The taproom is a single deep room with a long bar along the back wall, eight stools under it, a hearth on the west wall and loose tables everywhere else. The corner table under the bar's east end, beside the door to Olfard's back office, is Tarsh's by long custom; Olfard does not seat anyone else there. The office has its own door onto the yard, which is Tarsh's way out.

Patronage is mostly working harbor men: stevedores, junior officers off shore leave, dock-warden retirees, the occasional retired marine. The room runs busy from the seventh bell of evening through the eleventh, then thins. Tarsh arrives between the seventh and eighth bells most evenings he is in town and stays through the tenth or eleventh.

The approach

Read aloud — the Wreck

When the party first walks into the Coopered Wreck in the evening.

The Coopered Wreck is one long low room, black with forty years of coal smoke and loud the way rooms are loud when everyone in them has shouted on a deck all day. A long bar along the back wall with a row of stools under it; a hearth on the left; tables wherever tables would fit. Behind the bar a one-eyed man in his sixties is drying a cup that is already dry, and he watches you come in with the eye he has left.

The corner table at the far end of the bar, by a shut door, has one man at it. Thin, balding, a long pale face over a clay pipe, a heavy coat he has not taken off. There is an empty bench across from him, and the room is full, and nobody is sitting on it.

He takes the pipe out of his mouth, looks at you, and puts it back.

The party walks in. They will not be the first strangers who have ever been in the Coopered Wreck, but they will be the first strangers in a long while who walked directly to the corner table. Olfard will watch them from the bar. Tarsh will see them coming and stay seated.

Tarsh's first move is conversational, not violent. He is a broker; he assumes the party is here to hire him until they prove otherwise. "Sit down," he says, gesturing to the bench across from him. "Two of you. Tell me what brings you. The other three or four can stand at the bar. Olfard will pour them."

This is genuine. He believes himself to be safe at his own table, in Olfard's house, with at least one bodyguard within thirty feet (on Quiet Pursuit, no bodyguard; on Commercial Cover, one within a stone's throw outside the tavern's back door).

The conversation

Tarsh leads. He asks the party who recommended him. He asks what they need done. He asks how they pay.

The party can play this two ways:

1. Maintain the broker pretext (Deception)

The party pretends to be hiring him. This buys time and lets them ask questions in a frame Tarsh accepts. Useful for getting him to talk about how the firm pays him, who his Hardby contacts are, what he charges for what kinds of work. Insight DC 14: Tarsh is genuinely available for hire and is not currently on alert. Deception DC 16 to maintain pretext past five minutes — too many specific questions about Cindren & Vhal will tip him.

If the pretext breaks: Tarsh stands smoothly, says, "I think you are not here to hire me. I think you should leave my table." The party can then either escalate (see Confrontation below) or back off (Tarsh slips out the back within the hour and the party has lost the chance — though Veska's documents still name him).

2. Direct confrontation

The party shows him a piece of recovered evidence — a chop he applied, a name he transferred, anything from Veska's package that names him in writing — and tells him plainly what they want.

Tarsh's reaction is not panic. He sets his pipe down, looks at the document carefully, lets out a long thin breath of pipe-smoke through his nose, and says: "Well. That is a paper I would have preferred not to be holding."

Then he listens. He weighs. He answers questions in short careful sentences.

What he gives up

If the party has appropriate leverage (a smoking-gun document, witness testimony, or simply outnumbers him with witnesses present), Resh yields what he knows in exchange for a one-way passport out of Hardby and a written guarantee that his name does not appear in the eventual indictment. Caelith will honor this in writing if asked.

What he tells the party (in roughly this order, as they ask):

  1. Solen Mereth. "Yes. He runs the second set of books out of the Hardby branch. Has done since 580. I was his clerk when he started. He kept me on as outside contractor when I left."
  2. Tarlith Vhal Sereth. "The senior partner who signs off. I have never met him. Outside the partners' floor, almost nobody has — he has not signed a letter at his own desk in eleven years. I have carried two sealed packets to Solen on Sereth's instruction. I can describe Sereth's seal in detail; I have never seen his face."
  3. Tamsin Moraven. Tarsh confirms her location based on the travel approach: warehouse on Black Cog Lane (Quiet Pursuit), the Whitemoor Estate two days east (Commercial Cover), or — if asked late and Tamsin is already dead — confirms it was Solen who ordered the killing and Worth who did it.
  4. His payment chain. The firm pays him in untraceable cash, delivered weekly by a courier who is a different person each time. He suspects the couriers are run by Worth. He does not know how the firm pays Worth. Down the line he pays in trade-drafts on Dellow's at the Greater Market, never on Cindren & Vhal paper — which is why Merev Sarth's three drafts were not the firm's. For the far end of the cash, say Seed Repair 1.
  5. The Rel Astra contact — refused. Tarsh will not name his counterpart in Rel Astra, even with leverage. "That man," he says, "is not someone I will trade for a passport. Take what I have given you and go. If you press, I will say nothing else, and you will have made an enemy of me, and I would prefer not to be your enemy."

If they came by the First Travel Intermission, the third wharf is his and Ansel Lantry is his man, and he confirms both without interest. It is the circular he wants to see, and he reads it twice: "That is my wharf and my price. The paper is not mine. I do not write things down." It is the truth. See @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgWharf01]{The Third Wharf and the Drafts House}.

If combat starts

Tarsh fights only as a last resort and only to escape. His full statblock is in the Phase 3 NPCs compendium (CR 6, hand crossbow, smoke pellets, Cunning Action, Uncanny Dodge). On Quiet Pursuit he has no bodyguards in the tavern. On Commercial Cover, one bodyguard outside the back door (use Bandit Captain). On either approach, if combat starts in the Coopered Wreck, two paid harbor-district enforcers (Thugs) drinking at the bar will defend Tarsh while he exits through Olfard's back room.

Olfard himself does not fight. He stays at the bar, watches, and remembers everything.

If the party kills Tarsh

Strongly discouraged. See his dossier (Hardby NPCs → Anver Resh) for full consequences. Short version: the party loses a major source of corroboration and intel, and the firm assumes a third party is in play, which destabilizes Phase 4 in unpredictable ways.

Official Delegation note

If the party is on the Official Delegation approach, Tarsh has been moved upcountry and the Coopered Wreck confrontation does not happen. The party identifies him through paper trails (Veska's notes, the C&V vault if breached, Hesren's notebook if Hesren is recovered). They never confront him in person on this approach. However — if the party explicitly returns to Hardby in Phase 4 or later, Tarsh may have surfaced again at a different establishment, and a confrontation can be arranged then. He is not gone forever; he is only gone for now.

Tactical Map

Coopered Wreck — tactical map. The bar runs along the back wall; Tarsh's table is the corner one under its east end, beside Olfard's office door, and the office's door onto the yard is his way out. The street door is in the south wall.

District Map

Docks District, Hardby. The Coopered Wreck (Tarsh's haunt) is at the head of Black Cog Lane; Whalemarket Quay holds Veska Maelan's notary office.

pages.name: The Third Wharf and the Drafts House (First Travel Intermission)

text.content:
The Third Wharf and the Drafts House

GM page, First Travel Intermission only. For a party that carries Mattick Sarn's two facts, or the circular's own terms: the third wharf at Hardby, and trade-drafts on a Hardby house that is not Cindren & Vhal. Neither is needed to finish Phase 3. Both shorten it, and both belong to Anver Resh.

The third wharf

Hardby counts its wharves west from the Whalemarket steps. The third is an old timber wharf at the foot of Black Cog Lane, below the Coopered Wreck, where coasters and lighters tie up after dark with no harbour clerk on the boards. It is Resh's: where the firm's retrieved people and papers come ashore, and where the Whitemoor boat sails from at dusk every fifth day.

The man with the mark is Ansel Lantry, a lighterman in his forties with a pewter ring on his little finger and the crossed stroke cut into its face. He shows it to any master who asks for the man. He meets boats, takes delivery, sends a boy up the lane to the Wreck, and has never read anything he carried. Asked what the mark means: "It means I'm the man. It sorts things." (Use a Thug if it comes to that. He runs first.)

When the party first watches the wharf at dusk.

The third wharf is older than the two beside it, and nobody has mended it in your lifetimes. Black timber, a single lamp on a post at the landward end, and a smell of tar and wet rope and the Wreck's chimney coming down the lane behind you.

A lugger lies alongside with her sail furled loose, ready to go. A broad man in a lighterman's coat sits on a bollard beside her, eating something out of a paper with his fingers, and every so often he looks up the lane as if he is expecting someone and is not much bothered whether they come.

When a boy runs down to him he wipes his hand on his coat and holds it out, and the boy looks at the ring on it before he says anything at all.

  • Watching it (an evening or two; Stealth DC 12 to do it unremarked): the lugger leaves at dusk every fifth day with one passenger, the courier — two, one sailing in five, when a hard-faced woman in half-livery goes out with him; that is Reyna Worth — and comes back two days later, light but for her. The boy runs to the Coopered Wreck.
  • Following the boat east is the work of Varley's man, or Survival DC 14 in a borrowed boat, and it ends at the Whitemoor cove. That is a road to Tamsin that does not run through Resh.
  • Talking to Lantry. Intimidation DC 13, or 20 gp and Persuasion DC 12, gets the boat's day, "east, a day's sail, a wine-house that doesn't make wine," and the fact that the man at the Wreck pays him. Unless the party keeps him, he warns Tarsh within the day: +1 on the clock if he reaches the Wreck.
  • Taking the courier here, before he sails, keeps the order at Whitemoor at whatever it already is (see @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3InvestigJrn.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3InPgWhitem1]{Whitemoor — Running the Rescue}).

Mattick Sarn

  • Dead. Nothing comes to the third wharf. The Grey Fee's silence is the only report anybody makes.
  • The Grey Fee escaped. She limps into Hardby four days behind the Kestrel Wife, and Sarn goes to the third wharf to claim his hundred for confirmation by name. If the party is watching the wharf they can take him before he reaches Lantry. If they are not, he does: that is the one segment the hand-off allowed, +1 on the clock, a recognition the firm did not have to pay for.
  • Brought to Hardby a prisoner. He tries for the third wharf the first night anybody turns their back, and if he reaches Lantry it is the same +1. The clean ending is the Gynarchy's: a Pomarj freebooter handed to the harbour watch with Master Roke's log is a pirate, and the harbour court asks pirates very few questions.

The drafts house — Dellow's

Dellow's, Changers and Drafts keeps one of the benches in the money-changers' alcove on the north side of the Greater Market. Mistress Ottilie Dellow, sixties and Hardby-born, is honest within the meaning of the trade, and a draft on Dellow's is as good as coin anywhere on Woolly Bay — which is why brokers like them.

When the party first comes to her bench.

The money-changers' alcove is a long arcade along the north side of the market with a bench in every arch, and every bench has a scale and a strongbox and somebody behind it who has already looked at your boots.

The woman at Dellow's bench is small and upright and wears her spectacles on a chain. She weighs a stranger's coin before she looks at the stranger, and she looks at you for exactly as long as it takes to decide you are not here to change money.

"Drafts," she says, before anyone has said the word. "People who don't want to change money always want to talk about drafts."

  • What she knows. Merev Sarth's three drafts of two hundred were drawn on one standing account, and the circular's hundred "in trade-drafts at Hardby" would have been too. The account was opened two years ago, in the spring, in the name of an M. Otterly, factor, who is nobody. It is funded in cash, weekly, by a different hand each time, and drawn on by one man only: thin, fifties, a smoker's voice, and a clerk's signature.
  • Getting it. Show her a draft, Sarth's testimony or the circular's terms, and Persuasion DC 15 — DC 12 with Caelith's token shown in private, or with Zoria Weis's word. She will not open her book; she will confirm the shape. Reading the book behind her back is Sleight of Hand or Investigation DC 16, and a crime in Hardby: +1 on the clock if they are caught.
  • What it is worth. A paper road to Tarsh that does not run through Veska; proof that the Loftwick job and the hunt at sea were paid from the same Hardby account; and leverage at the Wreck: "Your account at Dellow's paid Merev Sarth." That is a paper with his hand on it, which is the Direct approach.
  • Where it stops. She knows nothing about where the cash comes from, and she has never heard of a letter agency. The trail ends at her counter, on purpose.

pages.name: Harbor Before Throne — The Operational Reveal

text.content:
The Office of Mercantile Records. Zoria Weis puts her finger on the page, and the slogan stops being a slogan.

The investigative beat that takes the Phase 2 slogan and turns it into operational law. Best run in Hardby, after Veska's reveal, with Zoria Weis as the bridge to the Gynarchy's harbor-commission registry. Read this carefully — the reveal is meant to clarify the conspiracy's eastern objective without yet naming the candidate harbor commissioners or the Aerdy claimant. That is Phase 4.

Where the reveal happens

The Office of Mercantile Records, on the Council steps in the Old Quarter. Zoria Weis works at the southwest desk, third in from the door. She receives the party in the late morning of an ordinary working day, having confirmed the agreed phrase ("The autumn ledger"). She brings them to a small reading room at the back of the Office where the harbor-commission appointment registry is kept.

What the registry shows

Read aloud or paraphrase as Zoria shows the party the open volume:

"Rel Astra's harbor commission has seven seats. They are filled by old Aerdi imperial appointment, two hundred years of practice and more. Three of the seats — the First, the Third, and the Fifth — are filled by the old houses, by appointment that the seated Overking confirms when he is seated and confirmed himself. The other four are appointed by the harbormaster of Rel Astra and the city's mercantile guilds. Those four are filled now and have been for years; nothing strange there.

The three old-house seats are different. They are filled now, on paper. But the three current holders are dead."

(She turns the page.)

"The First Seat: Lord Hessar Olm, deceased 582 CY of natural causes, no successor formally seated.

The Third Seat: Lady Mirin Vesh, deceased 583 CY in a fall on her own staircase, no successor formally seated.

The Fifth Seat: Master Ervan Dale, deceased 584 CY of a brief illness, no successor formally seated.

The seats sit vacant. By Aerdi practice, the city's harbor business has been conducted by the four mercantile-guild seats only, with the three old-house seats noted as ‘pending confirmation.' This is unusual but not yet illegal — the law allows three years of vacancy before a seat falls to ordinary process. The first vacancy is two years old this autumn. The second is fourteen months old. The third is six months old.

The Aerdy succession is, as everyone knows, a question. The Overking is old. There are three claimants seriously in play and a half-dozen whose mothers think they should be. When a new Overking is seated, he must confirm the three old-house harbor commissioners of Rel Astra before he can collect harbor revenue from the city. Confirmation requires the harbor commissioners to exist. Currently they do not.

Whoever has positioned candidates to be appointed to those three vacancies before a new Overking is named will hand the new Overking three pre-confirmed votes on the harbor commission, controlling the eastern revenue. Or, if those three candidates vote against confirmation, the new Overking has no harbor commission to confirm at all, and Rel Astra's harbor revenue stops feeding the imperial treasury until the matter is resolved. Either way, whoever owns those three seats owns the eastern question."

(She closes the volume.)

"That is what your slogan means. Harbor before throne, in Aerdi practical law, is the timing window before a new Overking is seated, in which old-house harbor commissioners can be appointed by the existing protocol — by the senior partners of Rel Astra's old commercial families, voting in convocation. Cindren and Vhal Rel Astra is one of those old families."

What the party should leave with

  • The conspiracy is positioning to seat three candidates on Rel Astra's harbor commission before the next Aerdy Overking is named — and the Overking, as Zoria will say if asked, is old but not dying this year. The pressure is not the succession. It is the paperwork. At least one of the three seats — the Third — is being held open by a ceremonial succession-deferral, and a deferral is an instrument with an end date on it. If it lapses, that seat fills by ordinary process and the convocation loses it. Zoria does not know the date. She knows that somebody filed it, and that somebody will have to file again.
  • The three current vacancies were created on schedule: each old-house commissioner died on a date that opened the seat in time for the seating window. Two years, fourteen months, six months. The deaths are not random. (GM: Mirin Vesh's "fall" was Reyna Worth's work; Ervan Dale's "brief illness" was Reln Pollow's understudy in Rel Astra; Hessar Olm's "natural causes" were natural and the conspiracy got lucky on the first one.   • Cindren & Vhal Rel Astra is one of the old commercial families with a vote in the appointment convocation. Tarlith Vhal Sereth is, by virtue of his rank, one of the senior partners eligible to vote. The Sereth signature on the Vandrell escrow is therefore not just a corrupt signature — it is the signature of a man positioning himself to seat three commissioners on the harbor of Rel Astra.
  • The party does not yet know which three candidates the conspiracy intends to seat. Phase 3 stops here. Phase 4 names them.

What this clarifies for the table

The Phase 1/2 slogan was atmospheric. Phase 3 makes it operational: the conspiracy is racing a calendar, and the calendar is its own. GM — the two dates, which govern the rest of the campaign: the conspiracy's preferred date is the appointment convocation it has been arranging all along, and that is Phase 4's business. Its outside date is written on the Third Seat's deferral in a hand the party will not be able to place — "Hold open until the second autumn after the next" — which resolves to autumn 586, two years from the morning they rode out of Loftwick. Everything from here to the end of the campaign happens inside that window. Do not state either date at the table in Phase 3; the party has earned the shape of the problem, not its calendar. They want their people seated on Rel Astra's harbor commission before a new Overking can stop them. The Phase 4 question becomes: who are the three candidates, and who is seating them, and how soon.

The party should leave Phase 3 understanding that they cannot afford to wait. Whatever Phase 4 looks like, it is on a clock that is not their clock — it is the Aerdy succession's clock, and the conspiracy is ahead of them.

  • Why "E." is involved. The conspiracy as the party understands it now is mercantile and political — three harbor seats, eastern revenue, succession leverage. Eclavdra's interest is older and stranger and not visible in Phase 3's frame. This is the Drow lineage thread. Hold it for much later.
